items.title: Ocean pH change since pre-industrial
items.claim: Surface ocean pH has fallen since the late 18th century. By approximately how much?

options.text: About 0.1 units (around 30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration)

items.reveal:
Mean surface ocean pH has declined from around 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times. The pH scale is logarithmic, so this is roughly a 26-30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration.

The IPCC SROCC (2019) projected further decline of 0.3-0.4 by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.
items.why: Small numbers on a log scale can correspond to large biological consequences.

items.title: Why the Montreal Protocol worked
items.claim: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances. By the early 2020s what is the projected outcome?

options.text: The ozone layer is on track to recover to 1980 levels around mid-century outside the polar regions
The hole has expanded since the protocol

items.reveal:
WMO/UNEP scientific assessments (2018 and 2022) report stratospheric chlorine peaking in the late 1990s and recovery to 1980 ozone levels by around 2040 outside polar regions; 2066 over Antarctica.

Unreported CFC-11 emissions detected in 2018 were largely addressed by 2021.
items.why: A small group of carefully targeted treaties has produced large measurable atmospheric outcomes.

items.title: Paris Agreement targets
items.claim: The Paris Agreement (2015) commits parties to holding warming below 2 C and pursuing efforts to limit it to what?
items.reveal:
Article 2 of the Paris Agreement specifies 'well below 2 C' and 'pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C'. IPCC's 2018 SR15 report assessed the 1.5 C pathway in detail.

In 2023 the global mean temperature anomaly briefly exceeded 1.5 C above pre-industrial.
items.why: Climate policy numbers carry technical meaning beyond their headline use.
